_comment: Every capability Astro must take a decision about, with the decision, the evidence for
what the current build does, and the owner.
TWO STATE FIELDS. `observed_state` is what the CURRENT legacy build does and is
evidence-backed. `state` is the Astro Next DECISION. They are separate so that 'an
inherited patch disables this' is never silently promoted into 'we decided to disable
this' — most of the entries below inherit a behaviour nobody chose.
`observed_state: NOT_BUILT` is not a synonym for DORMANT. Baseline finding 1 measured
that nothing links the Astro overlay into the build graph, so every Astro capability is
absent from today's binary through a build defect owned by #7. The validator rejects
DORMANT on a NOT_BUILT entry for exactly that reason.
TWO EDGE FIELDS, FOR THE SAME REASON. `blocks` means the named issue's design depends on
this entry's DECISION. `inputs_to` means the named issue READS this entry. They were one
field and it cost an epic's worth of apparent dependency: ten already-decided entries
declared `blocks: [11]`, which read as ten pending decisions #11 was waiting on, while not
one of the 35 INVESTIGATE entries named #11 at all. critical-subset-for-schemes.md measures
that and names the five items where the relation really is a prerequisite.
Validated and rendered by tools/policy/manifest.py. Schema:

states.KEEP: Ship the capability with upstream Chromium's implementation and provider.
states.REPLACE: The capability survives; the implementation or the provider does not. Names a replacement.
states.DISABLE_BUILD: The code is absent from the binary, through stable build configuration. Falsifiable by a symbol or string scan.
states.DISABLE_RUNTIME: The code IS in the binary and is deliberately never registered or reached. Asserts presence AND unreachability. Still a live endpoint for threat-model purposes.
states.DORMANT: Present, unreachable as a consequence of the surrounding arrangement rather than of a decision. Must name the mechanism and carry an expiry.
states.INVESTIGATE: No decision. Requires a specific question and the thing that answers it. Not permitted at release cutover.

features.rationale: Astro's account system. REPLACE and not KEEP for a reason that is not stylistic: oxy_auth_callback_handler.cc:31-32 reads `access_token` and `refresh_token` out of URL query parameters, which the epic forbids outright — such a URL reaches history, the omnibox, the referrer and anything the user copies. #16 rebuilds it on Authorization Code + PKCE with state and nonce.

features.blocks_reason: May a remote origin reach the trusted scheme? Decided: NO, and the scheme must not ship an auth host until the mechanism exists to enforce it. Measured: Chromium's guard against a web redirect chain landing on a privileged URL is content::IsSafeRedirectTarget (content/public/common/url_utils.cc:81-107), which rejects a target via HasWebUIScheme at :95 — and HasWebUIScheme reads a three-element literal, {chrome, chrome-untrusted, devtools}, at :27-31. That literal is in //content/public/common, has no ContentBrowserClient extension point (the renderer has none), and `astro` is not in it, nor in the function's kUnsafeSchemes set at :82-94. So IsSafeRedirectTarget returns TRUE for an https:// -> astro:// redirect and content/browser/loader/navigation_url_loader_impl.cc:1575-1577 does not raise net::ERR_UNSAFE_REDIRECT. Any HTTPS site — not merely auth.oxy.so — could 302 a top-level navigation to astro://auth/callback?access_token=<attacker's>, against a handler that reads credentials out of its own query string (src/chrome/browser/oxy/oxy_auth_service.h:22-23, oxy_auth_callback_handler.h:15): session fixation straight into the browser's identity store. Consequences for #11, in order: (a) milestone 1 registers the schemes with a diagnostic host and NO auth host, which needs nothing from #16; (b) no host that consumes a credential may ship on astro:// until IsWebUIScheme is generalised into a common-layer scheme store; (c) #16 rebuilds the flow on Authorization Code + PKCE so no token rides a URL, which removes the payload but not the redirect reachability — both are needed. What is NOT decided here is #16's identity architecture; only the scheme-transport bit is.

It needs a Chromium checkout, so it belongs with the real-checkout cases rather than the checkout-free suite; the cheap half — that Astro's own host names are unique among themselves — is enforced by tools/policy/manifest.py.
features.blocks_reason: #11 deletes the astro://-to-chrome:// alias, and the moment it does, `settings` and `whats-new` become two pages sharing one map key. The winner is whichever of chrome://settings and astro://settings the user opened last in that profile, because the source is added when the controller is constructed; the loser returns net::ERR_INVALID_URL. Order-dependent, per-profile, per-session, silent. #11 needs the rule before it removes the alias — not the full list of surviving chrome:// hosts, which is the point of adopting a rule instead.
features.notes: Measured once and worth carrying: no chrome:// host constant begins with `astro` (`git -C chromium/src show HEAD:chrome/common/webui_url_constants.cc | grep -c '"astro'` -> 0), so an astro- prefix is a sufficient condition for disjointness — but it is not the rule, because `alia` and `adblock` are already disjoint without it and astro://astro-settings reads badly. Disjointness is the rule; the prefix is one way to satisfy it.
